artifact.recommendation: Adopt tail-aware sampling: retain 100% of error traces and requests above the p99 latency threshold, while keeping a low random sample of normal successful traffic for trace-level latency analysis.
reasoning: The prototype exceeded the required 40% cost reduction by reducing stored trace volume by 55%, while preserving all injected errors and p99 traces.
Errors are rare but highly valuable: 0.7% of requests produce 46% of traces used in incident reviews, making uniform or head-based sampling likely to discard disproportionately useful evidence.
Very slow requests comprise only 1% of volume, so retaining all of them provides diagnostic value with limited storage impact.
More than 98% of volume is normal successful traffic, making this category the most effective place to reduce retention.
Independent, fully aggregated metrics preserve broad service-level latency measurement; sampled normal traces can supplement metrics with representative request-level detail.
The backend already supports retention decisions after span assembly, so the required tail-based policy is technically feasible.
considerations: Define “very slow” per service or endpoint where latency distributions differ; a single global threshold may misclassify traffic.
Choose and periodically validate the normal-traffic sampling rate against required confidence and granularity for service-level analysis.
Use unbiased random sampling for normal traffic and record sampling probabilities so downstream analysis can apply weighting.
Consider preserving additional high-value signals such as explicit exceptions, unusual status codes, retries, and selected critical-service traces.
Monitor sampler capacity and decision latency because tail sampling requires buffering traces until sufficiently complete.
assumptions: The prototype workload and injected failures are representative enough to predict production storage reduction.
A request above the p99 threshold satisfies the requirement to retain every very slow request.
The 55% stored-volume reduction translates sufficiently closely to at least a 40% telemetry-cost reduction.
Full aggregated metrics provide the primary service-level latency statistics, while retained traces support diagnostic and segmented analysis.
Tail-sampler infrastructure can reliably assemble traces and make decisions without dropping qualifying traces.
risks: Tail-sampler overload, buffer eviction, late spans, or incomplete traces could violate the requirement to retain all errors and slow requests.
A normal-traffic sample that is too small may be inadequate for low-volume services, endpoints, tenants, or narrow analysis windows.
Changing latency distributions can make static slow-request thresholds stale.
Storage volume may fall by 55% without an equivalent bill reduction if costs are driven materially by ingestion, processing, or minimum commitments.
Sampling only on final trace outcome may miss diagnostically important anomalies that are neither errors nor above p99.
evidence_needed: Production cost model separating ingestion, processing, buffering, storage, query, and contractual charges.
Production trial results confirming at least a 40% bill reduction and 100% retention of naturally occurring errors and very slow traces.
Statistical analysis establishing the minimum normal-traffic sample rate per service and analysis interval.
Load and failure testing for sampler throughput, memory use, late spans, restarts, and failover behavior.
Operational definition and update mechanism for per-service or per-endpoint slow-request thresholds.

artifact.recommendation: Use tail-aware sampling that retains 100% of error traces and requests above the p99 latency threshold, while retaining a lower random sample of normal successful traffic.
reasoning: The prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55%, exceeding the required 40% cost reduction, while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces.
Errors are only 0.7% of requests but provide 46% of traces used in incident reviews, so uniform or head-based sampling would discard disproportionately valuable diagnostic data.
Very slow requests comprise 1% of volume and can be explicitly retained by a tail-aware policy.
Because normal successful traffic exceeds 98% of volume, reducing its sampling rate captures most savings with less impact on incident diagnosis.
Independent, fully aggregated metrics preserve broad service-level latency analysis; a random normal-trace sample can support trace-level latency investigation.
The backend supports retention decisions after spans are assembled, making the policy technically feasible.
considerations: Define “very slow” using a stable per-service or route-specific threshold where appropriate; a single global threshold may poorly represent heterogeneous services.
Set the normal-traffic sampling rate using service volume and required statistical precision, with minimum quotas for low-volume services.
Preserve unbiased random sampling metadata and effective sampling rates so trace-derived estimates can be weighted correctly.
Monitor storage volume, tail-sampler capacity, decision latency, dropped spans, and retention accuracy after rollout.
Consider priority rules for additional rare high-value signals such as explicit failure status, exception events, or critical services.
assumptions: Telemetry cost is sufficiently correlated with stored trace volume for the prototype’s 55% storage reduction to satisfy the cost-reduction target.
The prototype behavior is representative of production traffic and scale.
The p99 threshold is available to the tail sampler and satisfies the requirement for retaining very slow requests.
Full-aggregation metrics provide the primary basis for service-level latency analysis, while sampled normal traces provide diagnostic detail.
Complete traces can be assembled reliably before retention decisions are made.
risks: Tail sampling requires buffering and state, increasing collector memory, latency, and operational complexity.
Prototype savings or retention accuracy may degrade under production load, burst traffic, or partial-trace arrival.
A normal sampling rate that is too low could weaken per-service, per-route, or low-volume latency analysis.
Dynamic p99 thresholds may lag incidents or create inconsistent retention behavior.
Retaining all errors and slow traces could cause cost spikes during widespread failures or latency events.
evidence_needed: Production-scale load-test results for tail-sampler throughput, memory use, decision latency, and incomplete-trace rates.
A cost model translating retained volume and sampler infrastructure overhead into net telemetry spend reduction.
Statistical precision requirements and minimum normal-trace sample sizes by service and route.
Validation that error and p99 retention remains complete during bursts and collector failures.
A capacity and budget policy for periods when error or slow-trace volume surges.

citations.claim: The prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces.
Errors are 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews.
Requests above the p99 latency threshold represent 1% of volume.
Normal successful traffic represents more than 98% of trace volume.
Metrics are collected independently at full aggregation and do not require retaining every trace.
The backend supports tail-based retention decisions after spans are assembled.

strengths: The recommendation directly addresses all three constraints: lower cost, preserve errors and very slow traces, and retain a random normal-traffic sample for latency analysis.
The reasoning correctly prioritizes rare, diagnostically valuable errors and slow requests while targeting the dominant normal-success traffic for reduction.
Claims are consistently tied to the supplied evidence, with accurate artifact locators and no external or unverifiable citations.
The report distinguishes aggregate metric analysis from trace-level diagnostic analysis.
Operational concerns are well identified, including buffering, late spans, overload, threshold drift, low-volume services, and failure-period cost spikes.
The proposed production validation, cost modeling, statistical sizing, and load/failure testing are appropriate prerequisites for rollout.
weaknesses: The recommendation does not specify an initial normal-traffic sampling rate, so it is not yet an executable policy.
It treats the prototype's 55% storage reduction as exceeding the 40% cost target in parts of the reasoning, even though storage reduction and bill reduction are not necessarily equivalent.
The policy does not specify how errors are identified across trace outcomes, span errors, exceptions, status codes, or application-specific failure signals.
The phrase "retain 100%" is operationally absolute, but the report does not define an availability or loss budget for collector failures, late spans, or malformed traces.
The rollout design lacks explicit acceptance criteria, rollback triggers, and a staged deployment plan.
unsupported: The assertion that uniform or head-based sampling is likely to discard disproportionately useful evidence is plausible but not directly demonstrated by a comparative test in the supplied evidence.
The claim that sampled normal traces will adequately support trace-level latency analysis is unsupported until required precision, service cardinality, time windows, and sample rates are quantified.
Technical feasibility at production scale is not established merely by backend support for post-assembly decisions.
The prototype establishes retention of injected test cases, not guaranteed retention of all naturally occurring qualifying traces.
No supplied evidence proves that a 55% reduction in stored traces yields at least a 40% reduction in total telemetry cost.
missing: An explicit initial sampling configuration, including normal-traffic rates or adaptive minimum sample quotas by service or route.
A precise definition of "error" and "very slow," including whether p99 is historical, rolling, per-service, per-route, or globally computed.
The time window, update cadence, and behavior during threshold warm-up or missing latency baselines.
A cost equation covering ingestion, processing, collector infrastructure, storage, indexing, querying, egress, and contractual commitments.
Statistical power or confidence calculations for normal-request latency analysis, especially for low-volume dimensions.
A production rollout plan with shadow evaluation, canary stages, dashboards, alerts, rollback criteria, and ownership.
Policy behavior during incident surges when errors or slow requests cease to be rare.
Treatment of trace completeness, duplicate decisions, multi-region routing, and late-arriving spans.
incorrect_assumptions: Equating p99 requests with every request that stakeholders intend by "very slow" may be wrong; the requirement does not formally define that term.
Assuming stored trace count or volume is an adequate proxy for total telemetry spend may be wrong when ingestion, processing, indexing, or fixed commitments dominate.
Assuming full-aggregation metrics are sufficient for all service-level latency analysis may be wrong if analysis requires tenant, route, version, or exemplar dimensions absent from metrics.
Assuming traces can always be completely assembled before a decision conflicts with the acknowledged risks from late, missing, or dropped spans.
Assuming prototype traffic and injected failures represent production scale, topology, bursts, and naturally occurring failures remains unvalidated.
critical_risks: Tail-sampler overload, eviction, restart, partition, or late-span behavior could drop precisely the error and slow traces the policy promises to retain.
Failure or latency storms could sharply increase retained volume and sampler memory requirements, undermining both reliability and the cost target.
An undersized normal sample could make low-volume service or route analysis statistically unusable despite healthy aggregate metrics.
Threshold lag or inappropriate global thresholds could omit diagnostically slow requests or retain excessive traffic.
The project could meet the storage-volume target while failing the required telemetry-bill reduction.
recommended_changes: Rephrase the decision as conditional on a production cost validation rather than claiming the prototype already satisfies the cost constraint.
Specify an initial normal sampling rate plus adaptive per-service or per-route minimum quotas, then justify them with confidence-interval or error-bound calculations.
Define error and slow-trace classification precisely, including threshold scope, time window, refresh cadence, warm-up behavior, and fallback rules.
Add a surge policy with reserved capacity, budget guardrails, prioritization, and explicit behavior when qualifying traffic exceeds capacity.
Run shadow and canary trials using natural production traffic; measure net cost, qualifying-trace retention, trace completeness, sampler resource use, and analytical precision.
Set measurable acceptance criteria and rollback triggers, including at least 40% net cost reduction and a clearly defined retention reliability target.
Resolve the artifact ambiguity: two nearly identical research reports are presented despite the instruction to review a single target report.

The reasoning correctly prioritizes rare, diagnostically valuable errors and slow requests while targeting the more than 98% normal-successful traffic category for savings.
Claims are traceable to the supplied evidence, and the citations accurately map the main factual assertions to e1–e6.
The reports appropriately distinguish full aggregated metrics used for broad latency measurement from sampled traces used for request-level diagnosis.
Important operational and statistical issues are recognized, including buffering, late spans, overload, threshold drift, low-volume services, sampling weights, and production-scale validation.
The reports correctly flag that reduced stored volume does not necessarily imply an equal reduction in the total telemetry bill.
weaknesses: The conclusion that the prototype exceeded the cost-reduction requirement is initially stated too strongly: it demonstrated a 55% reduction in stored trace volume, not a verified 40% reduction in total telemetry cost.
No concrete normal-traffic sampling rate or adaptive allocation method is proposed, so the policy is directionally correct but not yet deployable.
The recommendation treats retention above p99 as equivalent to retaining all 'very slow' requests without an explicit definition from the problem.
The reports do not define how errors are identified across partial or distributed traces, including exceptions, failed spans, application status codes, and transport failures.
The two research artifacts are nearly duplicative and provide little independent analysis or meaningful comparison of alternatives.
unsupported: The assertion that uniform or head-based sampling is likely to discard disproportionately useful evidence is reasonable but not directly quantified for the proposed alternatives or their actual retention probabilities.
The claim that sampled normal traces will adequately support trace-level latency analysis lacks sample-size, confidence-interval, service-volume, and analysis-window calculations.
Technical feasibility is only partially supported by backend capability; e6 does not establish that production collectors can reliably buffer and assemble traces at required scale.
Representativeness of the prototype workload, failures, trace sizes, and production scale is unproven.
The assumed relationship between the p99 threshold and the undefined category 'very slow requests' is unsupported.
missing: An explicit production cost model covering ingestion, processing, network transfer, collector infrastructure, storage, queries, and contractual minimums.
A specified normal-traffic sampling policy, including baseline rate, minimum per-service or per-route quotas, probability metadata, and adjustment rules.
A precise definition of error and very slow traffic, including threshold scope, calculation window, update cadence, and behavior when threshold data is unavailable.
A rollout plan with canarying, success criteria, rollback triggers, dashboards, and auditing of qualifying-trace retention.
Quantitative capacity planning for bursts in errors or slow traces and a policy for reconciling the 100% retention requirement with finite buffers or budgets.
Analysis of trace-size weighting: reducing trace count by 55% may produce a different byte-volume or cost reduction if retained error and slow traces are larger.
A direct comparison table showing why the 10% uniform and 1% head-based options fail the retention constraints.
Treatment of low-volume services, new services, and routes for which p99 estimates are unstable or statistically weak.
incorrect_assumptions: A 55% reduction in stored trace volume is implicitly treated in parts of the reasoning as proof that the telemetry-cost target is exceeded; the evidence establishes volume reduction only.
Equating 'above p99' with every 'very slow request' assumes a definition not provided by the decision problem.
Assuming trace assembly before storage guarantees complete tail decisions overlooks late, missing, or orphaned spans.
Assuming full aggregated metrics alone preserve every required dimension of service-level latency analysis may fail where analysis requires trace attributes or high-cardinality segmentation.
critical_risks: Collector overload, buffer eviction, restarts, late spans, or partitioning could cause qualifying errors and slow traces to be dropped, violating an absolute retention constraint.
Incident-driven surges may sharply increase the retained fraction precisely when errors and latency spike, causing cascading telemetry overload or unexpected costs.
The policy may meet storage-volume goals but fail the required bill reduction because significant costs occur before the retention decision.
An undersized normal sample may make route-, tenant-, region-, or low-volume-service latency estimates unreliable.
Stale or unstable p99 thresholds can under-retain genuinely slow requests or produce unpredictable retention and cost behavior.
recommended_changes: Reword the conclusion to say the prototype demonstrates promising storage reduction, while production cost compliance remains conditional on validating the full cost model.
Specify an initial normal sampling rate and a stratified or adaptive policy with minimum sample quotas by service and route, then justify it with precision calculations.
Define error and slow-request predicates operationally, including per-service or per-route thresholds, rolling windows, cold-start behavior, and fallback rules.
Add production-scale load, burst, failure, and late-span tests that measure qualifying-trace retention, not merely overall throughput.
Instrument sampling decisions with reason codes, effective probabilities, dropped-trace counters, and audits comparing eligible versus retained traces.
Model count, byte volume, and end-to-end spend under normal operation and incident surges, including sampler infrastructure overhead.
Establish capacity reserves and explicit behavior during overload; if 100% qualifying retention is truly mandatory, design durable buffering or redundant failover accordingly.
Run a staged production trial with predefined gates: at least 40% net cost reduction, verified retention of qualifying traces, and acceptable statistical precision for normal-traffic analysis.

attacks: The recommendation is not yet a valid policy: it specifies neither the normal-traffic sampling rate nor stratification, minimum quotas, adjustment rules, or required statistical precision.

The claimed constraint satisfaction conflates a 55% reduction in stored trace volume with a 40% reduction in total telemetry cost; tail decisions may occur after ingestion, processing, network, and indexing costs are incurred.
“Retain 100%” is unsupported operationally. Buffer eviction, overload, restarts, partitions, incomplete traces, and late spans can selectively lose the exact traces promised for retention.

Using requests above p99 as the definition of “very slow” is an invented interpretation. A rolling p99 also guarantees retention of roughly 1% even when performance is healthy and may lag abrupt regressions.
The prototype used injected errors and p99 traces; this does not establish retention of natural failures, partial traces, unusual error encodings, burst conditions, or production topology.
Tail-aware sampling can become least reliable and most expensive during incidents: error and slow-trace rates may surge simultaneously, exhausting buffers and eliminating expected savings.
Independent aggregate metrics do not prove that sampled normal traces support the required latency analysis. Metrics may omit route, tenant, version, region, or other high-cardinality dimensions.
The analysis ignores trace byte size. Error and slow traces may be larger than normal traces, so request fractions and trace-count reductions may materially overstate storage and cost savings.
Backend support for post-assembly rules establishes capability, not production feasibility, throughput, fault tolerance, or complete trace assembly.
The two research reports are effectively duplicates, so their agreement is not independent corroboration and should not increase confidence.
falsifiers: An end-to-end production billing trial shows less than 40% net telemetry-cost reduction after including ingestion, processing, transfer, indexing, querying, sampler infrastructure, and contractual minimums.
Shadow evaluation finds any qualifying natural error or defined very-slow trace missing because of classification errors, late spans, collector failure, overload, or incomplete assembly.
Production burst tests show buffers, decision latency, or retained volume exceeding capacity when error and slow-request rates rise together.
Confidence-interval analysis shows the proposed normal sample cannot meet latency-analysis precision for required services, routes, dimensions, or time windows.
Byte-weighted measurements show retained error and slow traces are sufficiently large that the prototype’s 55% trace-count reduction does not produce the required savings.
Stakeholders define “very slow” differently from above a rolling p99, invalidating the proposed retention predicate.
Comparative testing shows a simpler policy—such as head sampling combined with independent always-on error capture—meets all constraints with lower cost or operational risk.
Audit data shows errors cannot be identified reliably until after spans are missing, malformed, or discarded, making complete error retention impossible with the proposed architecture.
evidence_gaps: A full cost model and production invoice comparison, including costs incurred before tail sampling and added sampler infrastructure.
An operational definition of error and very slow, including scope, windows, refresh cadence, cold-start behavior, missing-baseline fallback, and partial-trace handling.
A concrete normal-traffic sampling configuration justified by sample-size and precision calculations for every required analysis dimension and interval.
Production-scale tests of throughput, memory, trace size, late arrivals, restarts, failover, partitions, and buffer eviction.
Retention audits using naturally occurring errors and latency events, with a measurable reliability target rather than an unqualified 100% promise.
Incident-surge modeling with capacity reserves, durable buffering, budget guardrails, prioritization, and explicit overload behavior.
Count- and byte-weighted traffic distributions by outcome, service, route, and trace complexity.
A direct experimental comparison against the two rejected options and plausible hybrid or stratified alternatives.
A staged rollout specification with acceptance gates, rollback triggers, observability of sampling decisions, and accountable ownership.
Evidence that full metrics contain all dimensions needed for service-level latency analysis and that sampled traces adequately cover dimensions they omit.

accepted_criticisms: The recommendation is directionally appropriate but not yet an executable policy because it lacks a normal-traffic sampling rate, stratification, minimum quotas, adjustment rules, and statistical-precision targets.
The report overstated constraint satisfaction by treating a 55% reduction in stored trace volume as evidence that total telemetry cost would fall by at least 40%.
An absolute promise to retain 100% of qualifying traces is unsupported without measured reliability and controls for overload, eviction, restarts, partitions, incomplete traces, and late spans.
Equating requests above p99 with all stakeholder-defined “very slow” requests is unsupported; the predicate, threshold scope, window, cadence, warm-up, and fallback behavior must be defined.
The injected-error prototype does not establish retention reliability for natural failures, unusual error signals, partial traces, bursts, or production topology.
Incident surges can simultaneously increase sampler load and retained volume, threatening both reliability and savings.
Independent aggregate metrics do not establish that sampled traces can support every required service-level latency dimension or precision target.
Trace counts alone are insufficient because retained error and slow traces may have different byte-size and processing-cost distributions.
Backend support for post-assembly rules demonstrates capability but not production-scale feasibility, complete assembly, throughput, or fault tolerance.
rejected_criticisms: The duplication of the two research reports is a valid process concern, but it does not undermine a claim of independent corroboration because the report did not rely on their agreement as independent evidence or use that agreement to justify confidence.

The criticism that a rolling p99 necessarily retains roughly 1% during healthy operation is not fully established by the visible evidence because the report did not specify a rolling threshold implementation; however, the broader objection that p99 was an invented definition of “very slow” is accepted.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select tail-aware sampling as the preferred policy architecture, but approve only a staged shadow and canary trial—not unconditional production adoption. Before rollout, define error and very-slow predicates; specify a statistically justified stratified normal-traffic sampling policy with minimum quotas; validate byte-weighted, end-to-end net cost savings of at least 40%; and demonstrate a defined qualifying-trace retention reliability target under production load, failures, late spans, and incident surges. Establish acceptance gates, overload behavior, capacity reserves, observability, ownership, and rollback triggers.
reasons: Tail-aware sampling remains the best-aligned option because it can prioritize the rare errors that contribute disproportionately to incident diagnosis while reducing retention of the more than 98% normal-successful traffic.
The prototype provides promising evidence of storage reduction and test-case retention, but it does not prove the total-cost, production-reliability, or analytical-precision constraints.
The original recommendation was too strong because it said the prototype exceeded the cost requirement when only stored trace volume was measured.

Neither uniform 10% sampling nor head-based 1% sampling can intentionally guarantee retention of all errors and slow traces, so the architectural preference remains unchanged even though deployment approval is now conditional.
Confidence is reduced because critical definitions, cost translation, sample sizing, trace-size distributions, surge behavior, and production failure testing remain unresolved.

accepted_criticisms: The recommendation is directionally appropriate but not yet an executable policy because it lacks a normal-traffic sampling rate, stratification, minimum quotas, adjustment rules, and statistical-precision targets.

A 55% reduction in stored trace volume does not prove the required 40% reduction in total telemetry cost; ingestion, processing, transfer, indexing, sampler infrastructure, and contractual costs require validation.
An absolute 100% retention promise is unsupported because overload, eviction, restarts, partitions, incomplete traces, and late spans can lose qualifying traces.
Treating requests above a rolling p99 as the definition of “very slow” is unsupported without stakeholder agreement and operational threshold rules.
Injected prototype errors and p99 traces do not establish retention reliability for natural failures, unusual error encodings, partial traces, production topology, or bursts.
Incident surges can simultaneously increase retained volume and sampler resource demand, threatening reliability and savings.
Independent aggregate metrics do not establish that sampled traces meet latency-analysis needs across required high-cardinality dimensions.
Trace-count reduction may overstate byte and cost reduction if retained error and slow traces are larger.
Backend support for post-assembly decisions establishes capability but not production-scale feasibility, fault tolerance, or complete assembly.
Production rollout gates, overload behavior, sampling-decision audits, and rollback triggers are missing.
rejected_criticisms: The near-duplication of the two research artifacts should not increase confidence, but it does not undermine the substantive tail-aware recommendation because that recommendation is supported directly by the problem evidence rather than by treating the reports as independent corroboration.

The criticism that retaining roughly 1% above p99 during healthy operation is inherently defective is rejected; that cost may be acceptable and diagnostically useful, although the threshold still requires an agreed definition and cost validation.

The absence of a direct experiment against every alternative does not invalidate selecting tail-aware sampling among the listed options: uniform 10% and head-based 1% sampling cannot guarantee retention of all qualifying errors and slow requests by design.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select tail-aware sampling as the preferred architecture, but approve only a shadow/canary production trial—not unconditional deployment. Define error and very-slow predicates; size a stratified normal sample with per-service or per-route minimum quotas and precision targets; test byte-weighted end-to-end cost, natural-event retention, completeness, burst capacity, and failure behavior; and deploy only if predefined gates demonstrate at least 40% net telemetry-cost reduction, the agreed qualifying-trace retention reliability, and adequate latency-analysis precision.
reasons: Tail-aware sampling remains the only listed option designed to preserve errors and slow traces while concentrating reductions on the more than 98% normal-success traffic.
Errors are rare but disproportionately useful in incident reviews, supporting outcome-aware retention.
The prototype provides promising evidence of storage reduction and test-event retention, but not proof of total-cost compliance or production reliability.
The original adoption language overstated constraint satisfaction by treating stored-volume reduction as cost reduction and injected-test retention as an operational guarantee.
Key predicates, statistical requirements, capacity limits, and acceptance gates must be resolved before this becomes a deployable policy.

artifact.decision: Select tail-aware sampling as the preferred architecture, but do not approve unconditional production deployment yet.
artifact.action: Authorize a staged shadow and canary trial. Advance to production only after predefined gates verify at least 40% end-to-end net telemetry-cost reduction, an agreed qualifying-trace retention reliability target, and adequate statistical precision for normal-request latency analysis.
reasons: Tail-aware sampling is the only listed option designed to preserve error and slow traces selectively while concentrating reductions on normal successful traffic.
Errors are rare but disproportionately valuable during incident review, making indiscriminate uniform or head sampling poorly aligned with the retention constraint.
The prototype is promising but proves only a 55% reduction in stored trace volume and retention of injected test cases; it does not prove total-cost compliance or production reliability.
The proposed policy is incomplete without operational definitions of error and very slow traffic, a statistically justified normal sampling configuration, overload behavior, and rollout gates.
The two research reports are substantially duplicative, so their agreement does not provide independent corroboration.
evidence: Problem e1 states that errors are 0.7% of requests but account for 46% of traces used during incident reviews.
Problem e3 states that normal successful traffic exceeds 98% of trace volume, providing the principal category from which to reduce retention.
Problem e4 states that the prototype reduced stored trace volume by 55% while retaining all injected error and p99 test traces.

Problem e5 states that metrics are collected independently at full aggregation, reducing dependence on complete trace retention for broad latency measurement, though dimensional adequacy remains unproven.
Problem e6 states that the backend can apply retention rules after spans are assembled, establishing basic support for tail decisions but not production-scale reliability.
Both rebuttals correctly narrow the recommendation to a conditional shadow/canary trial and explicitly require cost, reliability, and precision validation.
rejected_alternatives: Uniform 10% sampling would retain only a sample of qualifying errors and slow requests rather than intentionally preserving them all.
Head-based 1% sampling cannot generally classify requests using final outcomes or completed latency and would discard most qualifying traces absent a separate capture mechanism.
Immediate full production adoption is rejected because the visible evidence does not establish end-to-end cost savings, natural-event retention, production-scale resilience, or analytical precision.

Rejecting tail-aware sampling outright is premature because the supplied traffic distribution, incident-review value, prototype result, and backend capability make it the best-aligned listed architecture for further validation.
minority: A hybrid using head sampling plus independent always-on error capture could potentially reduce tail-sampler complexity, but it was not one of the evaluated options and no evidence shows that it preserves complete slow traces or satisfies all constraints.

A strict reading of 'all error traces and very slow requests' may make any finite, failure-prone telemetry architecture noncompliant; the practical requirement should be converted into a measurable reliability objective unless literal losslessness is mandatory.
unresolved: The operational definitions of error and very slow, including threshold scope, window, cadence, cold-start fallback, and partial-trace handling.
The normal-traffic sampling rate, stratification dimensions, minimum quotas, adjustment rules, and required confidence or error bounds.
The relationship between stored trace reduction and total telemetry cost after ingestion, processing, transfer, indexing, querying, infrastructure, and contractual minimums.
Retention and trace-completeness behavior during overload, restarts, partitions, late arrivals, malformed traces, and incident surges.
Count- and byte-weighted distributions of normal, error, and slow traces.

Production ownership, capacity reserves, audit instrumentation, acceptance gates, and rollback triggers.
assumptions: The decision is among the three listed options, with staged validation permitted before final deployment.
The requirement to keep all qualifying traces can be operationalized as an explicitly agreed, very high measurable reliability target unless stakeholders confirm literal losslessness.
Full aggregated metrics remain available independently as stated in problem e5.
No unshown cost model or production reliability evidence should be presumed.
change_conditions: Approve production deployment if a representative trial demonstrates at least 40% net end-to-end telemetry-cost reduction, meets the agreed qualifying-trace retention target under failures and surges, and satisfies latency-analysis precision requirements.

Reject or redesign tail-aware sampling if byte-weighted billing shows insufficient savings, qualifying traces are selectively lost, sampler capacity fails during bursts, or normal samples cannot support required analysis.
Prefer a simpler or hybrid architecture if comparative testing demonstrates equal constraint satisfaction with lower cost and operational risk.
Revise the retention predicate if stakeholders define very slow differently from requests above p99.
next_validation: Define error and very-slow predicates with service or route scope, threshold windows, refresh cadence, cold-start behavior, and incomplete-trace rules.
Design a stratified normal sample with minimum quotas and calculate precision for every required service, route, dimension, and time window.
Run shadow evaluation against natural production errors and latency events, auditing eligible versus retained traces and completeness.
Run load, burst, restart, failover, partition, late-span, and buffer-eviction tests, including simultaneous error and latency surges.
Measure trace counts, bytes, and all end-to-end cost components during representative baseline and canary periods.

Predefine rollout gates, rollback triggers, overload priorities, durable-buffering expectations, ownership, and review cadence.
